en: Verses for Encouraging and Inspiring All Kings,
composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of India during the Song Dynasty.
O King of Supreme Virtue, I have no other desire;
regarding the teachings spoken by all Buddhas, what is the essential meaning of their adornment?
I have briefly compiled these verses of the noble ones, which Your Majesty ought to hear.
Just as when an image of the Tathāgata is fashioned from various kinds of wood,
the wise pay it respectful homage and regard it with reverence because it represents the Buddha;
so now, through my own unrefined eloquence, I shall proclaim the treasury of reality.
The wise should have faith and delight, listening to what is spoken in accordance with the Dharma.
Although Your Majesty has heard the Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice discourse many times, supreme awakening arises from extensive learning; hearing it repeatedly leads to deep conviction.
Just as the sun illuminates white cloth, how could it not increase its brilliance?
The Triple Gem, generosity, and the heavens—the Most Victorious One has taught these six recollections.
Following after all such merits, one should observe them with perfect accuracy.
Always practice the ten paths of wholesome action through body, speech, and mind;
remain pure, stay far from alcohol that causes intoxication and confusion, and avoid wrong livelihood by practicing right livelihood.
Know that wealth is shared among five families and is impermanent and unstable.
Bestowing gifts upon those with virtue, the poor and suffering, and one's own kin—this merit follows one wherever one is born. Generosity is supreme:
it is neither interrupted nor extinguished; it is not abandoned, nor does it expect a fruit.
Thus, these various pure precepts should be properly received and maintained;
for they constitute a fertile field, from which all merits arise.
[They consist of] generosity, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and immeasurable wisdom.
These perfections should be cultivated by the wise;
they can cross the ocean of the three realms of existence and attain the state of the Honored Muni.
If a person is filial toward their parents and serves them with utmost sincerity, [they shall likewise attain this].
This is called the gateway of ritual and instruction; it is the pure, supreme lineage of the devas.
Its fame spreads far and wide, for those who cast off their bodies are reborn in the heavens.
One should abstain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and deception, as well as from drinking alcohol and the three types of unwholesome speech.

Having accomplished the eightfold perfection, following the training of all Buddhas, he relinquished his body and was reborn in the six heavens, where all his desires were fulfilled according to his will.
Greed, flattery, deceit, hypocrisy, and pride; laziness, craving, anger, and delusion—[he abandoned them all].
Noble lineage, a handsome appearance, youth, and great learning—
these various delusions should be viewed as enemies.
If one cultivates heedfulness, this is the path to immortality.
Heedlessness is the path to death; this is what the World-Honored One has taught.
For the sake of increasing wholesome dharmas, one should practice heedfulness.
If a person first commits evil but later becomes heedful, [they will attain purity].
This illuminates the world, like the moonlight revealed when the clouds have cleared.
Patience is peerless; it does not follow after a mind of anger.
The Buddha taught that one who can distance themselves from this attains the path of the Non-returner.
There are those who harbor anger like one drawing on water, and others like one drawing on earth or stone;
if one speaks of transcending afflictions, the first person is the superior.
One who reforms evil to cultivate loving-kindness and patience is the highest of all.
The Supreme One has taught that there are three kinds of speech regarding sentient beings:
the first is called "speech that captivates the mind," which is as sweet as honey;
the second is called "speech of truth," which is like the blooming of a wondrous flower.
The latter is called insincere; it is base and frivolous like excrement and filth.
The wise should discern this and abandon the latter while cultivating the first two.
From light to light until the end, from darkness to darkness to the ultimate.
Some pass from darkness into light, while others pass from light into darkness;
the wise should understand this clearly and, abandoning the three [lower realms], ascend to the first light.
Some appear ripe when they are unripe, while others appear unripe when they are ripe.
Sometimes both [the male and female organs] arise together; the wise discern this clearly.
Not gazing upon the form of another’s wife, even if one does gaze, one should regard her as a mother or a daughter.
Even so, if delusion still arises, one should cultivate the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
The mind and its thoughts are prone to wandering and distraction;
one should diligently and skillfully maintain them, as a person guards excellent learning, a precious treasure, a beloved child, or their own life.
One should regard the pleasures of the five desires as being like a venomous serpent.
Toward enemies, hatred, swords, and fire, One should skillfully cultivate weary detachment.
The five desires give rise to what is not meaningful, Just like the *bimba* fruit;
Their concealed appearance is a great deception, Binding people to abide in birth and death.
The wise should observe this: abandon it and do not be defiled.
The sense faculties are ever restless, racing toward the realms of the six objects;
if one can skillfully subdue them, that is true great courage.
This body is a walking latrine; the nine orifices constantly flow with filth.
It is porous and impossible to fill; a thin skin conceals its impurity.
The foolish are deceived by it, but the wise man should feel weary of it and seek liberation.
Like a person afflicted with scabies who seeks the warmth of a fire to relieve their suffering—
finding little pleasure while their pain subsequently increases— so too is it with sensual desire.
By skillfully understanding the faults of desire, one may thereby escape all suffering.
Those who wish to see the ultimate truth, The Buddha taught them to contemplate dependent origination;
They should practice it with diligent effort, For nothing is more supreme than this.
One of noble birth with a dignified form, Adorned by the garland of great learning—
If one does not cultivate ethical discipline and wisdom, this is not excellent;
yet to possess both of these virtues is truly marvelous, even if one lacks the other three.
Whether it be gain or loss, defamation or fame, praise or blame, and suffering or pleasure—
Unshaken by the eight worldly dharmas, such a one is a noble king. Do not,
for the sake of various devas, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kinsmen,
or guests, commit the evil karma of taking life.
When life ends, one enters hell, To suffer there alone, with no substitute.
If a person commits evil deeds, The bitter torments are not felt immediately;
But when life ends and the retribution for suffering arrives, What can be done then by subsequent regret?
Faith, precepts, generosity, and much learning, Wisdom, and a sense of shame and remorse— The Buddha has declared these to be unique treasures; All other wealth is shared with everyone.
Gambling, grand social gatherings, Laziness, and associating with evil friends—
Drinking alcohol leads to heedless dissipation;
wandering at night without shame—these six things defile one's reputation, and the wise should keep far from them.
Contentment is the greatest wealth, as proclaimed by the World-Honored One.
If one can practice contentment, though poor and lowly, one is truly great and wealthy.
Like a many-headed dragon, where there are many heads, there is much suffering;
with a nature of deep-seated resentment, she is called a wife who is an enemy.
Arrogant and disobedient, she is called one who treats her husband with contempt;
she squanders the husband’s wealth and is thus termed a "thieving wife.
Be cautious, O virtuous husband; you should keep far away from these three kinds of wives.
Compliance is her sister; affection is her good friend;
consolation is her mother; obedience is her servant.
These four virtuous wives are truly a husband’s kin.
Food and drink serve as medicine; do not consume them with greed, anger, or delusion.
Take them only to cease bodily suffering, not for the sake of fattening or indulgence.
Diligently cultivate your practice by day, and likewise during the first and last watches of the night.
In the middle of the night as well, maintain right mindfulness, And do not let empty dreams pass by in vain.
Cultivate the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity Day and night;
even if you have not yet transcended the world, Your merit will surpass that of the Brahmā heavens.
Free from sensual thoughts, they rejoice; practicing the four dhyānas amidst suffering and pleasure, they attain the fruit of the Brahma-light purity and experience the joys of these various heavens.
If a person commits little evil and extensively cultivates immeasurable goodness, [they shall enjoy such rewards].
Just as when a handful of salt is thrown into the great Ganges River;
if a person commits many evils but cultivates few pure merits,
it is like placing a great amount of potent poison into a small vessel of food.
The five aggregates are dark thieves, plundering the precious jewels of human goodness;
the five faculties, when fortified by faith, are capable of providing excellent protection against the sufferings of birth,
old age, sickness, and death, and the separation from those one loves.
Sinking and submerged without transcending to liberation—this arises from the fault of one’s own karma.
If you seek birth in heaven or liberation, you should diligently cultivate right view;
for even if one practices good deeds with wrong view, all will result in the fruit of suffering.
Impermanence, suffering, and impurity—these one should observe well.
If one does not engage in correct reflection, the four inversions will blind the eye of wisdom.
Beautiful forms are not the self, nor is the self the master of form.
The four aggregates are likewise so: they are merely an empty mass of suffering.
They do not arise at random, nor without cause;
they do not exist by way of intrinsic nature, nor are they produced by a creator god. They arise from ignorance, craving, and karma.
The view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt—these three are obstacles to liberation.
Through noble wisdom, one opens the gate of deliverance; this is achieved by one's own power, not through another.
By training in pure ethical conduct and meditative concentration, one diligently cultivates the four dhyānas.
One should always diligently train in the higher training of virtue, mind, and wisdom.
All virtues, knowledge, and meditative concentrations are entirely contained within these three trainings.
The Buddha taught that the power of mindfulness of the body is the path of the Single Vehicle.
One should always bind the mind in mindfulness and skillfully guard it;
if one forgets this right mindfulness, then all wholesome dharmas will be lost.
This body and life are extremely fragile and fleeting, like a bubble on the water blown by the wind.
Awakening from a dream cannot be guaranteed; the breath exhaled may not return.
In an instant, all becomes fine dust; know that nothing is solid or firm.
Even the great earth, Mount Sumeru, and the oceans will all be consumed by flames for seven days.
Everything has been utterly consumed without a single ember remaining; how much more so this fragile body?
Impermanence cannot be relied upon, nor is it a protective dharma.
This body is not to be trusted—how could one not feel weary of it?
For example, it is more difficult for a blind turtle in the ocean to encounter the hole in a floating log than it is for an animal to regain a human body. Why, then,
within the human realm, do you not cultivate the karma for supreme fruition?
To place filth within a precious vessel is the act of a foolish person;
yet to have obtained this precious human body and use it to perform evil deeds—
know that such a man is even more utterly foolish than that.
Born in a land where the Way exists, One encounters virtuous friends;
With right view and a perfected mind, One possesses merit from past lives.
Fully endowed with the wheel of the four jewels, One is able to leave the path of birth and death.
Those who draw near to virtuous friends and fully cultivate the holy life—
of such people the Buddha says that their minds are always in a state of tranquil extinction.
Those with wrong views and those in the three evil realms do not hear the sound of the Buddha’s Dharma.
In borderlands and regions of darkness, among the deaf, the mute, and the long-lived heavens—
O King, you have now escaped these eight difficulties and attained this unimpeded body;
you ought to cultivate wholesome deeds and employ skillful means to seek Nirvāṇa.
Within the long night of birth and death, amidst immeasurable and manifold sufferings, beings revolve as the six types of relatives;
their status as superior or inferior has no fixed order.
Throughout eternal kalpas of birth and death, there has never been one who has not been our child.
If one were to calculate the milk drunk from the breast of a compassionate mother, its volume would equal the four great oceans;
yet for an ordinary person about to undergo birth, the amount drunk is even greater than this.
The bones accumulated by a single individual since beginningless time would tower as high as Mount Sumeru.
All the humans and devas encountered along the way, as numerous as the atoms of the great earth—
some were previously wheel-turning kings and later became servants,
while others rose to be Śakra, served by all the gods.
Descending to be born amidst dung and soil, they wander back and forth countless times.
At other times they are born in the heavens, where they enjoy the utmost pleasure with celestial maidens;
their eyes dazzle at myriad exquisite forms, and their ears hear ten thousand kinds of sounds.
The body’s touch was entirely fine and soft, its bliss beyond description.
Later, falling into the hells, there was no bitter torment one did not undergo;
if born among the trees of the Sword Forest, head and body were severed by blades as they fell.
Sometimes they roam upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, ascending and descending according to their thoughts.
Together with many celestial maidens, they bathe in the Mandārava Pond;
adorned with rows of precious flowers, it is cool and refreshingly blissful.
Again they enter the River of Boiling Ash, where they are boiled and cooked until utterly mangled.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of the five desires in the six heavens, or the bliss of detachment in the Brahma worlds,
they die and enter the Avīci Hell, where they undergo every kind of bitter suffering.
Some become gods of the sun and moon, their radiance illuminating the four quarters;
yet later they are born in the dark hells, unable even to see their own forms.
Your Majesty, you should surely kindle the lamp of wisdom; do not continue to follow after the long-lasting darkness.
Within the eight great hells, one undergoes every kind of agonizing torment—burning, roasting, slaughtering, and tearing—asunder;
these immeasurable sufferings are beyond all comparison.
If a person follows delusion and confusion, they will fully commit a multitude of evil karmas.
If, in the interval before one has even exhaled again,
one hears of these various great sufferings and yet the mind feels no alarm or fear, such a person is but a block of wood or stone.
Even when seeing the manifestations of karmic retribution with one's own eyes and further hearing the explanations of the wise, [one remains unmoved].
One who merely collects the Buddha’s scriptures and reflects correctly within their mind should feel great dread;
how much more so for one who personally undergoes the practice!
Among all forms of suffering, none is greater than that of the Avīci Hell.
Among all forms of happiness, the exhaustion of craving is the supreme bliss.
Even if one were pierced by three hundred spears each day and night,
compared to the suffering of the Avīci Hell, it would not be even a hundred-thousandth part— a mere analogy cannot suffice.
Immeasurable torments and agonies, One seeks death but cannot find it;
One undergoes punishment for hundreds of thousands of years, Only when evil karma is exhausted does it end.
The impure and bitter retribution Has bodily and verbal actions as its seed.
If one does not sow, there will be no harvest; Your Majesty should sever the root of suffering.
If one falls into the realm of animals, there is the suffering of bondage and slaughter;
with minds crazed by greed and malice, they harbor enmity and devour one another.
For the sake of obtaining jewels, fur, tails, hides, flesh, or bones, they lose their lives;
they suffer the agony of being flayed and cut apart.
Those with swift feet and great strength endure the pain of having their necks pierced to be yoked for service and riding.
Wild and unruly, they are whipped and beaten with whips;
Hungry ghosts long for food and drink, yet what they crave never comes to be.
Pressed by hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, they find no rest throughout the long night.
Some have bodies like great mountains, yet their throats and mouths are like the point of a needle;
scorched within by hunger and thirst, they face food but find no way to eat.
Others see excrement, pus, and spittle, and run toward them in swarms, vying with one another to seize them.
Upon arrival, they are naturally extinguished; as hope is severed, their suffering increases.
Hunger and thirst sear their insides; goiters erupt and abscesses break out.
They further seize and claw at one another, gnashing their teeth and sucking at pus and blood.
Emaciated, with skin and bone joined together, naked and with long hair,
his body like a withered tree, blazing flames issue from his mouth,
burning his own body as if it were a *tāla* tree on fire.
In summer, one longs for the coolness of night, yet the moonlight increases the heat;
in winter, one thinks of the warmth of day, yet the rising sun freezes the ice even more.
Fruit on a tree withers away as one approaches it, and the river water dries up as soon as one goes toward it.
For fifteen thousand years, his karma sustained his life without ceasing.
Having long endured immeasurable suffering, this was due to the conditions of past transgressions;
various afflictions oppressed him, consisting purely of uninterrupted pain from the very beginning.
Covetousness, stinginess, and extreme attachment— The Buddha taught these to be the causes for rebirth as a hungry ghost.
Though the heavens may offer pleasure, When merit is exhausted, there is extreme suffering.
This is not the fruit of the noble ones; It is that upon which the wise do not rely.
The body lacks luster, one finds no joy in one's usual seat,
the flower crown suddenly withers and falls, dust and grime suddenly coat the body,
and sweat flows from beneath the armpits; know then that the time of death has arrived.
When the pure karma leading to happy rebirths is exhausted, one falls again into the three evil realms;
or one is born as an asura, constantly tormented by greed and jealousy.
Though possessing wisdom and intelligence, one ultimately does not perceive the True Reality.
Within the six realms of birth and death, one revolves without ever ceasing;
The supreme Dharma does not admit rebirth, for those who are born are vessels of manifold suffering.
Even if fire were to blaze from the crown of your head, maintain right mindfulness and do not harbor such thoughts.
One who has no karma for further existence should single-mindedly and diligently cultivate the precepts,
meditative concentration, and wisdom; being tranquil, disciplined, and unshakable,
one should seek the path to Nirvana, ultimately departing from birth and death.
Mindfulness, discernment, and diligence; Joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity— These seven factors of enlightenment Are the pure path to the deathless nectar.
Without wisdom there is no meditation, and without meditation there is no wisdom.
When both of these are accomplished, one can emerge from the stream of birth and death,
that boundless great ocean of suffering, regarding it as merely water in a cow’s footprint.
Regarding the fourteen points of the indeterminate, the Buddha taught that they should not be contemplated.
This is not the path of peace, nor is it the state of cessation.
Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by those, consciousness arises.
From consciousness, name-and-form emerge; the six sense bases have name-and-form as their cause.
From the six sense bases arise the six types of contact; from contact arise the various sensations.
Sensations are the cause of craving; from craving arise the four types of clinging.
From the four types of clinging arise the three modes of existence; with existence as the cause, subsequent birth occurs.
From birth come old age and death, Sorrow, lamentation, and all manner of suffering;
This immeasurable mass of misery Is utterly extinguished when birth is exhausted.
Thus has the Most Victorious One revealed The profound Dharma of dependent origination.
If one can observe correctly, upon the basis of true vision—
such true vision as this is itself the seeing of the Buddha.
Right view and right intention, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Right mindfulness, right effort, And right samādhi—these eight factors of the noble path Should be cultivated for the sake of peace and cessation.
Birth is the truth of suffering; Attachment and affection are its origin.
The cessation of suffering is called liberation; reaching that state is the Eightfold Path.
To perceive those true realities, one should always diligently cultivate right wisdom;
though dwelling amidst the pleasures of the five desires, the wise are able to transcend them.
Those who can realize the True Dharma all arise from the state of ordinary beings;
they do not descend from empty space, nor do they emerge from the earth.
The wise and fearless King grasps the essential point without waiting for further elaboration.
One should repair the bridge of the True Dharma to cross over the abyss of birth and death.
Since these aforementioned profound dharmas are difficult to perfect even for those who have left the household life,
how much more so for a ruler of the world— how could such a person be able to practice them fully?
Cultivate practice gradually according to the occasion, and do not let the days pass in vain.
When all people cultivate goodness, always give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy;
perform the three types of action yourself, and correctly dedicate them toward the Buddha-way.
In future ages, they shall receive this immeasurable merit;
constantly born among gods and humans, they shall become sovereign kings.
Together with a multitude of great bodhisattvas, they shall sport in various supernormal powers.
Using skillful means to transform sentient beings, They adorn and purify the Buddha-lands.
With generosity, precepts, and wisdom as their seeds, They travel back and forth among humans and devas.
Their stainless and pure reputation Spreads throughout the lands of the ten directions.
The Guide and Lord of the World, appearing above as a Heavenly King, causes them to renounce the pleasures of the five desires and remain far removed from all negligence.
Sentient beings are deluded regarding the true ferry; they drift and toss about, following the four currents.
The immeasurable suffering of birth and death— I shall deliver them to the further shore.
By this cause, may I attain the Buddha-way And reach ultimate great nirvāṇa.
This is the essential verse for exhorting and inspiring kings.
